**www.woodmac.com** **Copper: A market under pressure – the final curtain or just the intermission?** Richard Wilson, Chairman of Metals 24th May 2012, Tokyo **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Agenda** **1 Production disruptions and new project analysis 2 Some light at the end of the tunnel for custom smelters? 3 Indonesia – impact of proposed concentrate export ban 4 China – slowing growth, but should this worry us? 5 Deficits to surpluses – implications for copper prices** © Wood Mackenzie 2 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Will production disappoint again in 2012?** **One of the key factors that differentiates a copper market that remains undersupplied compared with the oversupply situation that is seen in the other base metals markets is the ongoing inability of copper mines to meet their production targets** **Over the past 8 years, mine disruptions due to pit wall failures, strikes, technical issues, slow ramp up of projects etc. have pared primary supplies by 6%, or around 1Mt/a Cu** **Based on disruptions identified to date in 2012 it does seem as though mine production will disappoint once again this year** **We estimate that ~250kt of mine output has been lost thus far in 2012 with operations affected by bad weather (northern Chile, Kazakhstan and Zambia), strikes (Zambia), technical issues (Chile, DRC and PNG) and slow ramp up of operations (Indonesia, Chile)** © Wood Mackenzie 3 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Will production disappoint again in 2012?** ## **Copper mine disruptions (2004 – 2012 YTD)** 3.7% 7.4% 6.8% 5.7% 8.0% 5.8% 5.0% 5.8% 1.3%

We estimate that 3Mt/a of greenfield, brownfield and restart capacity were committed to in 2010** **The abnormally high level of mine capacity additions in 2012 is a reflection of the catch up in mine developments following the deferra

ls post 2007** **The average addition to mine capacity over the 5 year period 2008 -2012 is 1.1Mt/a which is exactly the same level seen in 2007 prior to the FC** **Importantly, the additions to mine capacity tails off significantly post 2012 such that by 2015 the addition rate declines to 500kt/a** © Wood Mackenzie 5 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Copper mine capacity additions in 2011 & 2012 offset deferrals post 2008 FC** Average capacity addition (2008 - 2012) = 1.1Mt/a

© Wood Mackenzie **6** **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Light at the end of the tunnel for custom smelters?** **We have observed that in the past, when copper in concentrate production exceeds 88% of primary smelting capacity, concentrates tend to accumulate in the system, leading to market surpluses (as was last seen in 2004 and 2005)** **The combination of an ongoing shortfall in mine production due to disruptions and uncontrolled additions to Chinese primary smelting capacity led to a major reduction in available primary feed to smelters, most notably since 2008, resulting in depressed TC/RCs However, China has removed the responsibility for smelter project approval from the provinces and has centralised this function under the Ministry of the Environment. As a consequence, far fewer Chinese primary smelter projects are being given EIS approval and this has resulted in slower growth in project additions in that country** **With mine supplies set to rise significantly over the next few years at a time when growth in primary smelting capacity is being constrained, there will be a marked improvement in primary feed supplies to smelters from 2013 and this should be accompanied by higher TC/RCs** © Wood Mackenzie 7 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Light at the end of the tunnel for custom smelters?** Copper in Concentrates Availability Relative to Primary Smelter Capacity

**www.woodmac.com** # **Proposed Indonesian concentrate export ban could upset market equilibrium** **Indonesia’s net copper concentrate export potential ~2.5Mt/a by 2015** **The country’s one smelter (Gresik) can meet Indonesian cathode requirements through 2018 – its smelter capacity is equivalent to 137% of existing domestic demand** **Direct employment at Gresik is low (~500) cf. Grasberg (~9000) and Batu Hijau (~4000) Gresik is the only domestic acid supplier. Other acid needs are mainly met through burning sulphur (added benefit of power generation)** **A 200kt/a Cu Indonesian greenfield smelter would cost ~$1.2Bn requiring long run TC/RCs of 50-60c/lb (2012$) to generate a reasonable return** **Our long-term TC/RC forecast is 23c/lb (2012$)!** **Indonesia needs 2-3 greenfield smelters to fully absorb domestic concentrates production – basis the above, difficult to justify extra smelting capacity either commercially or economically** Export Ban

However, the correlation between IP and refined consumption is far less obvious in a China context. The extreme volatility for China reflects an economy that is still very much in an initial growth mode with the oscillations in copper demand being the result of variable infrastructure spending, various stimuli programmes, the availability of scrap and also China’s evolving net trade in semis products** **One has to question the significance of a 0.5% reduction in China’s annual GDP in terms of how this might impact copper demand, given the lack of correlation between economic growth and copper consumption** © Wood Mackenzie 10 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **No pattern to Chinese copper consumption…unlike in the world ex-China** 15%

Source: Wood Mackenzie © Wood Mackenzie **11** **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Chinese year on year consumption growth rates tell only part of the story** **We believe that to focus upon year-on-year Chinese copper consumption growth rate forecasts only tells part of the story in this rapidly growing market** **The following chart highlights year-on-year Chinese copper consumption growth averaged over successive 5-year time periods. It can be seen that for the past twenty years, Chinese refined consumption growth has averaged ~13% p.a.** **One of the biggest concerns for the copper market moving forward is the anticipated substantial reduction in Chinese copper consumption growth in the coming years** **Our own forecasts predict that over the next 5 years Chinese refined consumption growth will slow to 6.8% p.a. compared with 14.4% p.a. over the prior 5 years, which is a major reduction reflecting a transition towards a more consumer-driven economy** **However, in absolute tonnage terms, the 6.8% p.a. growth over the next 5 years actually translates into an increase in demand of 600kt/a compared with 760kt/a over the prior 5-year period** **Add to this the projected 300kt/a incremental demand growth in the rest of the world, this means that copper supplies will need to grow by an average 900kt/a to satisfy demand (mine capacity additions by 2015 are projected to be 500kt/a)** © Wood Mackenzie 12 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Chinese year on year consumption growth rates tell only part of the story** 800 14.4% p.a. 16.0%

t while estimates for the following 5-year plan have also been raised, by 42%** **The Chinese power market is an important consumer of copper and it can be seen that official estimates of spending (and hence demand) are consistently conservative** © Wood Mackenzie 14 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Chinese forecasts are often conservative, e.g. power investment** RMB trillion

However, massive buying by Chinese speculators and the SRB reversed the fortunes of the market in that year** **With a large increase in mine supply projected in the short term, this is a concern for the market because rising metal inventories could force prices lower. In 2011 the annual average copper price was 94% above marginal costs and this could imply a significant decline in copper prices is possible under deteriorating market conditions** © Wood Mackenzie 16 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Copper prices well above marginal costs – potential for a sizeable correction?** 100 Average Stocks 10000

Low inventories also leave the market exposed to unwelcome manipulation** **The following chart shows that our projected metal surpluses should bring metal inventories closer to normal levels by 2016 and prices closer to our long-term projection of $3/lb** **In the medium term, marginal production costs are unlikely to be a key influence on prices, because project incentive prices of $3/lb or higher will be required to ensure that future supply growth will match ongoing demand requirements** © Wood Mackenzie 20 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Prices & stocks trending towards long-term levels over the medium term** Metal Stocks (days of consumption) LME Price (c/lb - 2011$)
